flawed_step: Step 3: the claim that every finite unit-distance graph has a proper 3-coloring. This fails: the Moser spindle is a 7-vertex unit-distance graph that cannot be 3-colored.
counterexample: Moser spindle. Put A=(0,0). Rhombus 1: B and C are at distance 1 from A and from each other, and D is the reflection of A across line BC, so |AD|=√3. Rhombus 2 is rhombus 1 rotated about A by the angle θ that makes |DG|=1, where G is the image of D. This θ exists because the circle of radius √3 has a chord of length 1. The rotated points are E, F, G. Unit edges include AB, AC, BC, BD, CD, AE, AF, EF, EG, FG, DG. Suppose a proper 3-coloring exists. Triangle ABC uses all 3 colors, and triangle BCD shares edge BC, so col(D)=col(A). In the same way col(G)=col(A). Then col(D)=col(G), but DG is an edge. Contradiction.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt, with a check on each step:
1. Let G be any finite unit-distance graph. We want a proper 3-coloring. — Fine: this just sets up the goal.
2. Adding edges can only make coloring harder, so it would be enough to 3-color the full unit-distance graph on any finite point set. — Fine, and it matches the definition (an edge exists exactly when the distance is 1).
3. Claim: every such graph has a proper 3-coloring, for example by a greedy or planar-style argument. — NOT JUSTIFIED, and in fact false. No valid argument exists. Unit-distance graphs can contain K4-free pieces that force a 4th color. Greedy coloring only gives max degree + 1 colors, and a unit-distance graph need not be planar or 2-degenerate in a way that gives 3 colors.
4. Check with the Moser spindle (construction in the counterexample field). The points exist, since √3 > 1/2 means a chord of length 1 on the circle of radius √3 exists. The 11 listed pairs are all at distance 1. — Justified by basic geometry.
5. In any proper 3-coloring, triangles ABC and BCD share edge BC, so A and D must get the same color. By the same argument A and G get the same color. — Justified: in a triangle all 3 colors appear, so the vertex opposite BC gets the one color B and C don't use.
6. So D and G get the same color, but |DG|=1 makes DG an edge. This contradicts step 3. — Justified.
7. Conclusion: the first clause, "every unit-distance graph is 3-colorable", is false. The definitions say refuting it is enough. The second clause is also false: known results give a chromatic number of the plane of at least 5 (de Grey 2018). Even without that, the spindle alone gives at least 4, not 3. — Justified.
The proof breaks down at step 3, and steps 4–6 show the statement is false.
